etymology.text: From Middle High German gān, gēn, from Old High German gān, gēn, from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną. Cognate with Dutch gaan, English go, Swedish and Danish gå, Yiddish גיין (geyn).

funFacts: gehen and English go are one Germanic verb (Dutch gaan, Swedish gå).
Greek πηγαίνω and Turkish gitmek do not care how you travel; German splits it into gehen (on foot) and fahren (by vehicle) – exactly like Russian идти / ехать.
pitfalls: gehen is going on foot; by car, bus, train or ship you fahren: Ich fahre mit dem Bus. “Ich gehe nach Berlin” sounds like walking there (or, in speech, moving there to live).
Irregular in the past: ging – gegangen, and the perfect takes sein: Ich bin nach Hause gegangen.
Imperative: Geh! (du) – Geht! (ihr) – Gehen Sie! (polite).
subtleties: Without a destination gehen often means “to leave”: Ich gehe jetzt. = I’m off now.
Wie geht es dir? – literally “how does it go for you?”: gehen is impersonal here, with the dative dir / Ihnen.

governs.none: takes no object (where to and where from are adverbials: nach Hause, aus Berlin)

etymology.text: From Middle High German quëmen, komen, kumen, from Old High German quëman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-. Cognate with Dutch komen, English come, Danish komme.

funFacts: kommen goes back to the same Indo-European root *gʷem- as Greek βαίνω (to go, step) and Latin venire – the gʷ became k in Germanic, b in Greek and v in Latin.
pitfalls: kommen is movement towards the speaker (or the place in the story): Kommst du zu mir? – but Ich komme! (“I’m coming!”) also answers someone who calls you, as in English.
Irregular past kam – gekommen; perfect with sein: Er ist gekommen.
Origin with aus: Ich komme aus Athen (not *von Athen).
subtleties: Woher kommst du? asks for your origin; the colloquial split form is Wo kommst du her?
Imperative Komm! / Kommt! / Kommen Sie! – softened with doch or mal: Komm doch mit!

etymology.text: From Middle High German loufen, from Old High German hloufan, loufan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan. Cognate with Dutch lopen, English leap and lope, Danish løbe.

funFacts: laufen is English leap and lope; the noun der Lauf (run, course) gives Lebenslauf – “life-run” = CV.
The Dutch cognate lopen also means “to walk” – Dutch and German keep the walking sense that English leap lost.
pitfalls: Two meanings: in everyday speech laufen is “to walk, to go on foot” (Ich laufe nach Hause); in sport and with speed it is “to run”. When it must be clear, say zu Fuß gehen (walk) or rennen (run).
Stem change a → äu in du and er/sie/es: du läufst, er läuft – but the imperative has no umlaut: Lauf! (not *Läuf!).
Perfect with sein: Ich bin nach Hause gelaufen.
subtleties: Ski laufen (to ski) and Schlittschuh laufen (to skate) are also built with laufen.
laufen also says that things work or are on: Der Film läuft im Kino. Der Motor läuft.

etymology.text: From a merger of transitive / causative Old High German rennan (“to make something run or flow”) and intransitive Old High German rinnan (“to run or flow”). A similar merger shows in Dutch rennen and English run.

funFacts: rennen and English run come from the same pair of old verbs (“to run” and “to make run”), which merged in both languages.
pitfalls: rennen is always fast; for jogging or a race distance German usually says laufen: Ich laufe zehn Kilometer.
Mixed verb: rannte – gerannt (vowel change and -te like a weak verb); perfect with sein.
subtleties: das Rennen is a race (Autorennen = car race); der Rennwagen = racing car.

etymology.text: From Middle High German varn, varen, from Old High German faran, from Proto-West Germanic *faran. Cognate with Dutch varen, English fare, Danish fare.

funFacts: fahren is English fare (as in farewell = “travel well!” and the bus fare): both once meant simply “to travel”.
The noun family is huge: der Fahrer (driver), die Fahrkarte (ticket), das Fahrrad (bicycle), die Fahrt (trip), die Erfahrung (experience – what you get by travelling).
pitfalls: gehen is going on foot; by car, bus, train or ship you fahren: Ich fahre mit dem Bus. “Ich gehe nach Berlin” sounds like walking there (or, in speech, moving there to live).
Stem change a → ä in du and er/sie/es (du fährst, er fährt) – but not in the imperative: Fahr! (not *Fähr!).
Perfect: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren (movement, sein) – Ich habe das Auto gefahren (driving something, haben).
subtleties: German does not mark who drives: Ich fahre nach Berlin = I go to Berlin (by train, car, bus …). To say you are the driver: Ich fahre (das Auto) / Ich sitze am Steuer.
For planes German uses fliegen: Wir fliegen nach Athen.

etymology.text: From Middle High German reisen, from Old High German reisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *raisōn, further from Proto-West Germanic *raisu (akin to Proto-Germanic *raizijaną).

funFacts: das Reisebüro is a travel agency and der Reisepass a passport – literally a “travel pass”.
pitfalls: du reist, er reist: the -s- of the stem swallows the -st ending (not *reisst).
reisen takes sein in the perfect: Wir sind nach Spanien gereist.
Do not confuse reisen (to travel) with reißen (to tear) – ß!
subtleties: reisen sounds like longer journeys; for an everyday trip Germans say fahren: Ich fahre am Wochenende zu meinen Eltern.

etymology.text: zurück- (“back”) + kommen (“to come”).

funFacts: zurück is literally “to the back” (zu + Rück-, as in der Rücken, the back) – the same picture as English “back”.
pitfalls: Separable: the particle zurück goes to the end of the clause: Ich komme morgen zurück. – Komm bald zurück!
zurückkommen = come back (towards here); to go back (away from here) is zurückgehen or zurückfahren.
subtleties: In the infinitive and the participle the verb is one word: Ich will zurückkommen. – Ich bin zurückgekommen.
Ich bin gleich zurück (sein + zurück) is an everyday way to say “back in a minute”.

profile.feeling: A knock at the door – “Come in!” – someone entering the room where you are.

to enter, to step in: Bitte treten Sie ein.
to enter (a room, a building) – transitive: Er betritt den Raum; also on signs: Betreten verboten!

etymology.text: herein- (“in, hither”) + kommen (“to come”); herein is her (“towards the speaker”) + ein (“in”).

funFacts: her and hin work like old English “hither” and “thither”: English lost them, German uses them every day (woher, wohin, herein, hinein).
pitfalls: her- = towards the speaker, hin- = away from the speaker: herein (in here, you are inside) – hinein (in there, you are outside).
Separable: Kommen Sie herein! – Ich komme herein. – but: Darf ich hereinkommen?
subtleties: Spoken German shortens both herein and hinein to rein: Komm rein! – Geh rein! – so the her/hin difference is mostly kept in writing.
The one-word answer to a knock is Herein! (Come in!).

contrasts.value: go in, away from the speaker outside

to enter, to step in

etymology.text: hinein- (“in, thither”) + gehen (“to go”); hinein is hin (“away from the speaker”) + ein (“in”).

funFacts: Greek μπαίνω and Turkish girmek are one verb for “enter”; German builds it from a direction word + a verb of motion: hinein + gehen, herein + kommen, rein + fahren.
pitfalls: hinein (in there – away from you) vs herein (in here – towards you): Ich gehe hinein. – Kommen Sie herein!
Separable: Ich gehe hinein. – Geh hinein! – but in the infinitive one word: Ich will hineingehen.
subtleties: In everyday German you mostly hear the short form rein: Ich geh mal rein.
Often the prepositional phrase is enough and hinein is left out: Ich gehe in den Laden.

profile.feeling: Leaving a place – going away; and, for young people, going out at night.

senses.def: to go away, to leave (a place) – intransitive

etymology.text: From weg- (“away”) + gehen (“to go”).

funFacts: weg comes from in Weg (“on the way”) – the same as English away = on way.
pitfalls: weggehen has no object: Ich gehe weg. – To name the place you leave, use verlassen: Ich verlasse das Büro (or: Ich gehe aus dem Büro).
Separable: Ich gehe jetzt weg. – Geh weg! (Go away! – can sound rude).
subtleties: Wann gehst du weg? can mean “When are you leaving?” or “When are you going out tonight?” – context decides.

contrasts.value: with an object: to leave a place or a person (das Haus verlassen)

profile.feeling: Walking out of a door, a city, a person – leaving something or someone behind.

senses.def: to leave (a place) – transitive: das Haus verlassen
to leave, to abandon (a person)
sich verlassen auf: to rely on

examples.text: Ich verlasse das Haus um sieben Uhr.
examples.tr: I leave the house at seven o’clock.

examples.text: Bitte verlassen Sie den Zug.

to depart (vehicles, travellers)

etymology.text: From Middle High German verlāzen, Old High German firlāzan, from Proto-West Germanic *fralātan, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Cognate with Dutch verlaten and archaic English forlet. Equivalent to ver- (“for-”) + lassen (“let, leave”).

funFacts: ver- is the German twin of English for- (forget, forsake): verlassen is literally “for-let”, to let go away.
pitfalls: verlassen needs an object (what you leave): Ich verlasse das Büro. – Without an object say weggehen or gehen: Ich gehe jetzt.
Not separable: ver- stays on the verb: Ich verlasse … – and the participle has no ge-: verlassen.
Stem change in du and er: du verlässt, er verlässt; perfect with haben: Ich habe das Haus verlassen.
subtleties: The participle is also an adjective: ein verlassenes Dorf (a deserted village), Ich fühle mich verlassen (I feel abandoned).
In announcements and signs it is the formal word: Bitte verlassen Sie das Gebäude.

senses.def: to arrive
es kommt auf … an: it depends on …

examples.tr: The train arrives at eight o’clock.

examples.text: Wann kommst du in Berlin an?

etymology.text: From Middle High German anekomen, from Old High German anaqueman, from Proto-West Germanic *anakweman, from Proto-Germanic *anakwemaną (“to come to, come at, arrive”). Compare Dutch aankomen, English oncome.

funFacts: an + kommen is the same build as English “on-come” (oncoming) and Dutch aankomen.
pitfalls: Separable: the particle an goes to the end: Der Zug kommt um acht Uhr an. – Not *Der Zug ankommt.
Where you arrive is wo? + dative: in Berlin, am Bahnhof, in der Stadt – not the accusative (it is a place, not a direction).
subtleties: Es kommt darauf an (it depends) is one of the most frequent uses of the verb.
Die Ankunft (arrival) is the noun on timetables, opposite die Abfahrt (departure).

etymology.text: From Middle High German blīben, belīben, from Old High German bilīban (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch blijven, archaic English belive.

funFacts: bleiben comes from the root *leyp- (“to stick”), as does Greek λίπος (fat) and German Leben (life) – staying is “sticking” to a place.
pitfalls: bleiben takes sein in the perfect, although nothing moves: Ich bin zu Hause geblieben.
Where you stay is dative (wo?): Ich bleibe im Hotel – not *ins Hotel.
English “stay at a hotel” as a guest is often übernachten or wohnen: Wir wohnen im Hotel Sonne.
subtleties: Duration takes the plain accusative: Ich bleibe eine Woche. – Wir bleiben zwei Tage.
stehen bleiben = to stop (walking); Bleiben Sie dran! = Hold the line! (on the phone).

examples.tr: I’m waiting for the bus.

etymology.text: From Middle High German warten, from Old High German wartēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wardēn, from Proto-Germanic *wardāną. Cognate with Old Saxon wardōn, Swedish vårda, English ward.

funFacts: warten is English ward (to guard, watch over) and warden; German still has der Wärter (attendant, guard) – waiting was once “keeping watch”.
pitfalls: Wait FOR = warten AUF + accusative: Ich warte auf dich (not *für dich).
Stem in -t: an -e- comes before -st and -t: du wartest, er wartet, ihr wartet; imperative Warte! (with -e).
English “I have been waiting for 20 minutes” = present tense in German: Ich warte seit zwanzig Minuten.
subtleties: das Wartezimmer (waiting room at the doctor’s), die Warteschlange (queue).
Na warte! (Just you wait!) is a playful threat.

lexemes.role: where to? – the question of direction (Wohin gehst du? → nach Hause, in die Stadt, zum Bahnhof)

synonyms.nuance: the split spoken form: Wo fährst du hin?

etymology.text: wo (“where”) + hin (“thither, away from the speaker”).

funFacts: English once had the same three words: where, whither (= wohin), whence (= woher); German still uses all three every day.
Hebrew has the same three questions: אֵיפֹה (where), לְאָן (where to), מֵאֵיפֹה (where from).
pitfalls: wo asks for a place (Wo bist du? – Im Park), wohin for a direction (Wohin gehst du? – In den Park). English uses “where” for both!
The answer to wohin takes the accusative after the two-way prepositions: in den Park, auf den Markt – and nach / zu + dative.
subtleties: Spoken German often splits it: Wo gehst du hin? – the hin goes to the end like a separable particle.

lexemes.role: where from? – the question of origin (Woher kommst du? → aus Griechenland, vom Bahnhof)

profile.feeling: Looking back down the road – where someone comes from, where a thing comes from.

senses.def: where from? – asking for origin or starting point

etymology.text: wo (“where”) + her (“hither, towards the speaker”).

funFacts: woher is English “whence”, wohin is “whither” – words English has almost lost.
Turkish builds the same idea with a case suffix: nereden? (where from?) – nere-den, the ablative.
pitfalls: The answer: aus + dative for countries, cities, buildings (aus Griechenland, aus dem Haus); von + dative for people and points (vom Bahnhof, von meiner Mutter).
Woher kommst du? asks for your origin – the present tense is used, as in English “Where are you from?”.
subtleties: Woher weißt du das? is not about places: “How do you know that?”.

etymology.text: From Omnibus, with influence from English bus.

funFacts: Bus is short for Latin omnibus, “for all” – a vehicle for everybody; the word went from French to German and English in the 19th century.
pitfalls: By bus = mit dem Bus (dative), not *mit Bus: Ich fahre mit dem Bus.
Plural with double s: der Bus – die Busse; genitive des Busses.
subtleties: im Bus = inside the bus (Ich lese im Bus.); mit dem Bus = by bus.
You get on einsteigen and off aussteigen: Ich steige am Bahnhof aus.

etymology.text: From Middle High German zuc, zug, from Old High German zug, from Proto-West Germanic *tugi, from Proto-Germanic *tugiz, an abstract noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”). Cognate with Dutch teug, English tug. Related to ziehen (“to pull”).

funFacts: Zug belongs to ziehen (to pull), like English tug and tow – the train is literally “the pulled thing”.
pitfalls: On the train = im Zug (not *auf dem Zug); by train = mit dem Zug.
Plural with umlaut: die Züge, dative den Zügen.
subtleties: Zug is “a pull”: a train is what is pulled; a draught is air that pulls; a chess move pulls a piece. Context tells the meaning.

etymology.text: From Flug (“flight”) + Zeug (“stuff, gear, device”).

funFacts: Flugzeug is a native German compound, “flight gear”, while Greek αεροπλάνο and English aeroplane go back to French aéroplane – German often builds its own word where other languages borrow.
pitfalls: With a plane the verb is fliegen, not fahren: Ich fliege nach Berlin.
Neuter: das Flugzeug (because das Zeug is neuter).
subtleties: das Zeug (stuff, gear) builds many devices: das Fahrzeug (vehicle), das Werkzeug (tool), das Spielzeug (toy).

The first petrol car was patented in Germany by Carl Benz in 1886.
pitfalls: Neuter: das Auto, plural die Autos (with -s, as many short loanwords).
Auto fahren is written as two words.
subtleties: mit dem Auto = by car; im Auto = inside the car.
German says Auto in speech and writing; Automobil is old-fashioned or technical.

etymology.text: From fahren (“drive/ride”) + Rad (“wheel”). Compare Dutch rijwiel.

funFacts: The ancestor of the bicycle, Karl Drais’s “Laufmaschine” (running machine), was ridden for the first time in Mannheim in 1817.

Plural with umlaut: die Fahrräder, dative den Fahrrädern.

etymology.text: From Middle High German schif, from Old High German skif (“ship, barrel, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą. Cognate with Dutch schip, Yiddish שיף (shif), English ship, Danish skib.

funFacts: Schiff and English ship are the same word; English skipper comes from Dutch schipper, “ship-man”.
pitfalls: Schiff (ship) is big, Boot (boat) is small – German keeps them apart like English.
On board = auf dem Schiff (not *im Schiff, unless you mean below deck).
subtleties: The ferry to an island is die Fähre; for it Germans also just say Schiff: Wir nehmen das Schiff nach Mykonos.

etymology.text: Via Middle Low German bōt, from Middle English bot (compare modern English boat).

funFacts: German Boot was borrowed from English boat via Low German – one of the early English loanwords in German.
Das Boot (1981), the film about a German submarine, made the word known worldwide.
pitfalls: Neuter: das Boot; plural die Boote.
Boot (small) ≠ Schiff (large): Mit dem Boot fährt man auf dem See, mit dem Schiff über das Meer.
subtleties: Boot fahren is “to go boating” for fun; to get somewhere you fahren mit dem Boot.

gut zu Fuß sein: to be a good walker, to be able to walk well

examples.text: Ich gehe zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: I walk to work.

examples.text: Zum Bahnhof sind es zu Fuß zehn Minuten.
examples.tr: It’s ten minutes on foot to the station.

examples.text: Meine Oma ist noch gut zu Fuß.
examples.tr: My grandma still walks well.

collocations.tr: to walk, to go on foot

synonyms.nuance: to walk (verb): Ich laufe. = Ich gehe zu Fuß.
on foot – jokey Latin

etymology.text: From Middle High German ze vuoze (literally “to foot”). Compare Dutch te voet.

funFacts: Greek says με τα πόδια (with the feet), Turkish yürüyerek (walking) – German uses the old dative of one foot: zu Fuß.
pitfalls: zu Fuß, not *mit dem Fuß or *mit Fuß: Ich gehe zu Fuß. (mit is for vehicles: mit dem Bus).
zu Fuß gehen is usually just gehen: Ich gehe zur Arbeit already means on foot; zu Fuß stresses it.
subtleties: Fuß is spelt with ß (long vowel); in Switzerland, which does not use ß, it is zu Fuss.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: The ticket machine at the station, the conductor’s “Ihre Fahrkarte, bitte!”

senses.def: ticket (for a bus, train, tram – a fare)

examples.text: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Hamburg.
examples.tr: I’m buying a ticket to Hamburg.

examples.text: Die Fahrkarten, bitte!
examples.tr: Tickets, please!

examples.text: Wo kauft man hier eine Fahrkarte?
examples.tr: Where do you buy a ticket here?

synonyms.nuance: ticket – now the everyday word, also for trains (Deutsche Bahn sells “Tickets”)
ticket – the word of transport companies and signs
ticket – Swiss

etymology.text: fahren (“to travel”) + Karte (“card”).

funFacts: Fahrkarte is literally a “travel card”; die Karte comes from Latin charta, from Greek χάρτης (a leaf of papyrus) – also the source of English card and chart.
pitfalls: Fahrkarte is for buses, trams and trains; for a plane, a concert or a film say Ticket (Flugticket) or Karte (Kinokarte).
Feminine because of die Karte: die Fahrkarte, plural die Fahrkarten.
subtleties: Riding without a ticket is schwarzfahren (“to ride black”), and the fine is heavy.

contrasts.value: any ticket: flights, concerts, also trains (everyday)

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Plane tickets, concert tickets, an app on the phone – the modern, international word.

senses.def: ticket (plane, train, concert, match)
ticket (in IT support: a request)

examples.text: Hast du schon ein Ticket für das Konzert?

examples.text: Ich kaufe die Tickets online.
examples.tr: I buy the tickets online.

examples.text: Das Ticket ist auf meinem Handy.
examples.tr: The ticket is on my phone.

examples.text: Ich habe beim IT-Support ein Ticket aufgemacht.
examples.tr: I’ve opened a ticket with IT support.

synonyms.nuance: ticket for bus, tram and train – the traditional word
admission ticket (museum, concert)
ticket (short): zwei Karten für heute Abend

etymology.text: Borrowed from English ticket.

funFacts: English ticket comes from Old French estiquet (a label) – the same word as étiquette and as German Etikett (label).
pitfalls: Neuter: das Ticket; plural die Tickets.
A parking or speeding ticket is not Ticket but der Strafzettel.
subtleties: Ticket is spreading fast: Deutsche Bahn now sells “Tickets”, but older people and signs still say Fahrkarte.
